paper.title: Exploring the Effect of Segmentation on a 10-bit DAC
paper.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of segmentation on the DNL (differential non-linearity) and INL (integral non-linearity) of a 10-bit differential output current-steering digital-to-analog converter (DAC), implemented in a 40 nm, 2.5 V, CMOS process. The achievable DNL improvement was characterized by simulating all intermediate degrees of segmentation possible between a binary and a thermometer implementation. The DNL results ranged between (-0.467, +0.474) LSB and (-0.024, +0.026) LSB with the INL remaining almost invariant at (-0.376, +0.345) LSB. A differential output current of +/-1mA was achieved for a circuit with an active analog area of 0.01 mm2. All decoder variants required for driving the analog content of the DAC have been physically implemented with their area documented. The theoretical results for the DNL and INL are compared with the Monte Carlo simulation results and are shown to be within a 30% margin of error.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

verdict.summary: Simulation-based design-space study of DAC segmentation with proportionate textbook formalism; two related self-citations, no released netlists or scripts, and limitations acknowledged only in passing.

## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Exhaustive Monte Carlo characterisation of all ten binary/thermometer segmentation splits of a 10-bit current-steering DAC in 40 nm CMOS, plus synthesis and place-and-route areas for the matching binary-to-thermometer decoders, compared against literature formulas for sigma_DNL and sigma_INL.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** Applies known segmentation theory and known mismatch-based estimation formulas (taken from lecture notes [11] and Pelgrom-style mismatch) to a new technology node. The contribution is an empirical validation and area table, not a new method.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 2 numbered (binary-weighted output current sum; Pelgrom mismatch relation) plus a table of six sigma formulas

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 0
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate. The equations are the standard engineering relations the paper sets out to test against simulation; removing them would remove the object of the comparison.

### Issues
None identified for formalism. Minor inconsistencies: the purely thermometer variant is labelled "01B10T" in one place and "00B10T" elsewhere; the relative-error range in the text, (-30.70, -11.55)%, does not match the last row of Table 6 (-11.66%).

---

## Citation Analysis

13 references; 2 self-citations: [6] the authors' own CAS 2020 conference version of this study (directly related; this paper is its extension) and [9] a 1985 Romanian textbook on electronic measurement instruments co-authored by M. Bodea, cited for the usual range of thermometer bits (marginal but on-topic). SCR about 15%, at the boundary of normal and elevated. The theoretical sigma formulas rest on a university lecture handout [11] rather than a peer-reviewed source.

---

## Structural Analysis

Claims are tied to tables (Table 5 areas, Table 6 computed vs simulated sigmas) and figures; the 30% error claim is supported by Table 6. All results are simulation-only (200 Monte Carlo runs); no silicon measurement. Limitations are acknowledged inline only: the finite number of Monte Carlo runs and the systematic overestimation by the formulas. No netlists, layouts, or Matlab scripts are released.

---

## Conclusion

A competent, modest extension of a conference paper. Formalism is proportionate and necessary. The main weaknesses are the absence of measured silicon, reliance on a lecture handout for the formulas under test, and no released artifacts.

paper.title: An algorithm-based method for accurate compensation of bandgap references over temperature
paper.abstract: A curvature-compensated bandgap voltage reference circuit, with a high degree of temperature compensation, is designed and implemented in a 0.18um CMOS technology. The accuracy of the circuit was obtained with the help of a software code, having the aim of calculating the necessary parameters. Thus, a newly design method, implemented in MATLAB software, is proposed. The circuit is intended for integration within a voltage regulator with an adjustable output voltage. The bandgap circuit provides a reference voltage of 1.2V, for supply voltages between 1.65V and 3.6V, over a temperature range of -40C to 85C. The targeted TC is below 10 ppm/C for typical process parameters.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text; the MATLAB design code is described through flow diagrams only

verdict.summary: Piecewise-linear curvature-compensated bandgap with a MATLAB parameter-sweep script; proportionate circuit equations, but the "algorithm" is a set of while-loops, the code is not released, and some performance claims are overstated.

## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Design of a 1.2 V bandgap reference in 0.18 um CMOS using the known piecewise-linear curvature-correction technique (Rincon-Mora), with two nonlinear currents; resistor and mirror coefficients are found by a MATLAB script that iteratively adjusts values with while-loops until slopes match.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** An existing compensation technique applied to a new design, with a straightforward iterative parameter search. The "algorithm" is described by the authors themselves as "basic programming statements (if and while)".

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 6 (VBE temperature dependence, piecewise nonlinear current, output voltage expressions, TC definition, figure of merit)

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 0
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate. The equations are standard circuit relations that the MATLAB script evaluates; they are needed to reproduce the design.

### Issues
None identified for formalism. Consistency issues: the abstract states a targeted TC below 10 ppm/C, Table 1 specifies below 20 ppm/C; the conclusions give the supply range as 1.8-3.6 V while results are reported from 1.65 V.

---

## Citation Analysis

9 references; 1 self-citation ([1], the authors' own CAS 2020 version of this work, directly related). SCR about 11%. Reference [9] does not appear to be cited in the text. No issues of concern.

---

## Structural Analysis

Simulation results over temperature, supply, process corners and Monte Carlo are tabulated and support the TC and line-sensitivity numbers. However, several claims lack support: that the code "gives the best results" and that design time was "considerably reduced" are asserted without any comparison or timing data. The figure of merit comparison mixes simulated results for this work with measured silicon from others. Limitations are acknowledged inline: the algorithm ignores side effects, the op-amp offset is uncompensated, and trimming may be needed. The MATLAB code, the paper's stated contribution, is shown only as flow diagrams and is not released.

---

## Conclusion

A routine but adequate circuit design paper whose novelty claim rests on a simple iterative script that is not made available. Formalism is appropriate. Structural integrity is weakened by unsupported efficiency claims, internal specification inconsistencies, and simulation-only validation.

paper.title: A Novel Full-Wave Current Sensor for Automotive Synchronous Buck Converters
paper.abstract: This paper presents a novel full-wave current sensor based on the Vds-sense technique, suitable for fully integrated complementary switching power stages such as those used in synchronous buck DC-DC converters. It is designed to operate over a wide range of input voltages required by automotive applications. Provisions have been made for both current- and voltage-output, as well as for trimming. The novel sensor was derived by addressing the main limitations of a solution published previously by the authors. Both the circuit topology and circuit implementation were improved in order to increase the sensor accuracy. The new topology is simpler and allows for the signal paths to be implemented by using low-voltage transistors; the main transconductors were implemented by using the common-gate topology, which provides large bandwidth for a relatively low power consumption. A design example is presented in some detail: a full-wave current sensor for synchronous buck DC-DC converter designed in a High-Voltage 180nm CMOS process. The converter provides a nominal 5V output and up to 500mA, while the input voltage varies between 6V and 45V. Simulation results shown that the current sensor presented here operates over the entire range of input voltages and resulting duty-cycle, between 10% and 80%. The relative error when the signals driving the power switches have a 50% duty-cycle is under 1.2%pkpk for inductor currents larger than 200mA and remains below 7.2%pkpk down to 50mA.

verdict.summary: Incremental topology improvement of the authors' own Vds-sense current sensor, validated by simulation against re-implemented and published sensors; proportionate formalism, modestly elevated self-citation, no artifacts.

paper.title: New Constant-gm circuit for precision chopper offset-stabilized operational amplifiers
paper.abstract: The paper presents a low-voltage chopper offset-stabilized operational amplifier with a new constant-gm technique, having a 1.8-5.5 V supply range, designed and simulated in a 0.25 um CMOS process. The amplifier has an offset voltage of +/-5 uV, minimum CMRR of 106 dB, minimum PSRR of 121 dB, 51 nV/sqrt(Hz) voltage noise density and 550 kHz unity-gain bandwidth. The quiescent current is only 36 uA and was obtained due to the new low current constant-gm technique, which provides a variation of only 4% of the input transconductance and almost constant unity-gain bandwidth within the common-mode voltage range.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

verdict.summary: Low-current constant-gm input stage integrated into a chopper op-amp, with extensive PVT and Monte Carlo simulation; proportionate formalism, related self-citations, limitations stated, no artifacts.

paper.title: Microheater optimized for the integration with metasurface-based IR sources for gas sensing application
paper.abstract: This paper presents the design, manufacturing stages, electrothermal analysis and characterization of micro-heaters with platinum (Pt) resistive layer in four geometric configurations, which can be integrated with metasurfaces absorbers with applications in gas detection. The results obtained according to the electrothermal analysis and the performed experiments show that the studied micro-heaters can be integrated with metasurfaces to obtain the IR emission, necessary for gas detection.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

verdict.summary: Design, COMSOL simulation, fabrication and thermal characterisation of four Pt microheater geometries; textbook heat-transfer equations, related self-citations, qualitative agreement claims, no artifacts.

**Topic:** Four Pt meander microheater layouts on fused silica intended to double as the metal back-plane of a metasurface IR emitter for CO2 sensing; COMSOL electrothermal simulation, fabrication flow, R(T), steady-state and transient thermal measurements.
**Level:** 2 (Low)

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0
- Theorems: 0

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 0
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate in count. The equations are textbook background (cited to [15]) and are not used quantitatively afterwards, since the design is done in COMSOL; they are background rather than theater patterns.

### Issues
The radiation term is written with ΔT^4 and the Stefan-Boltzmann constant given in W m^-2 °C^-4, which is physically incorrect (radiation depends on T^4 - T0^4 in kelvin). Table 1 gives electrical conductivity in kg/m^3. These are presentation errors rather than formalism theater.

18 references; 2 self-citations: [13] Tomescu et al. on metasurface IR emissivity control (directly related) and [14] Paun et al., the CAS 2020 version of this work (directly related). SCR about 11%. No issues.

## Structural Analysis

Simulation and measurement are both presented, and Fig. 12 overlays measured and simulated temperature vs voltage. Agreement is described as "very good" without a quantitative error figure, and uniformity is judged visually from IR images. The integration with the metasurface, which is the paper's motivating novelty, is not demonstrated: no emission spectra are reported. A limitation is acknowledged inline (the 1 cm2 active area was dictated by the test set-up and will be reduced to cut power). No data or design files are released.

---

A competent device-engineering report with appropriate, if partly erroneous, background physics. The claims about suitability for metasurface integration go further than the evidence, which covers only the heater.

paper.title: Manipulation of particles using dielectrophoresis in a microchannel
paper.abstract: Over the years several methods were used to separate cells within a microfluidic device such as cavities, with vortex microfluidics method, or cell trapping mechanisms using size filters. However, one of the methods that is widely used to separate cancer cells from blood cells is the dielectrophoresis. In this work we employ the numerical code COMSOL Multiphysics for a dielectrophoretic separation of CTCs (circulating tumor cells) from RBCs (red blood cells) in a 3D microchannel. The microfluidic device is composed of one inlet and three outlets. The non-uniform alternative electric field is generated using interdigitated electrodes and it separates the cells within the device to the corresponding outlet. The electric field frequency was set to 100 kHz. For this paper, one single CTC line is selected MDA-MB-231, breast cancer cells. The CTCs and the RBCs are considered in an ideal way in the simulation as spheres, but with the afferent characteristics. This work can be extended to testing multiple CTC lines at various flow velocities and electric field frequencies

Calculated complexity: 0

Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate in count. The equations restate the physics COMSOL solves; they are textbook background rather than a contribution, but they are not theater patterns.

### Issues
None identified as theater. Several internal inconsistencies: the inlet velocity is given as 500 um/s, 180 um/s and "500 m/s" in different places; at 100 kHz both particles are said to experience negative DEP yet "remain attached to the electrodes", which contradicts the paper's own description of negative DEP pushing particles away from high-gradient regions; only one particle of each type is simulated.

11 references; 2 self-citations: [8] the authors' CAS 2020 paper this work continues (directly related) and [4] a magnetophoretic manipulation system co-authored by M. Avram (related as an active-separation example). SCR about 18%, elevated. Reference [1] is incomplete (no venue or year).

## Structural Analysis

The only experimental validation is a micro-PIV velocity profile of the flow field, without a quantitative comparison to the simulation. The separation claims rest on single-particle simulated trajectories. The conclusion that high frequency gives "better results" is undercut by the authors' own statement that 4.5e8 Hz is not experimentally obtainable without damaging cells; this is the main limitation acknowledged inline. No model files or data are released.

---

## Conclusion

A preliminary simulation study with minimal experimental support and internal contradictions in the reported results. Formalism is background physics and not inflated; structural integrity is the main weakness.

paper.title: A Standalone System for Resistive Smart Sensors Based on a Wheatstone Quarter-Bridge
paper.abstract: This paper presents the architecture of a resistive smart-sensor based on a Wheatstone quarter-bridge. The overall system also comprises a signal-conditioning circuit and a microcontroller. The intended sensing element is a small-variation chemo-resistive sensor. Its resistance gradient is converted by the conditioning circuit into a signal with variable duty-cycle. The proposed architecture is theoretically analyzed and validated by both simulations and measurements on a prototype, implemented with discrete and low-cost components. The output signal exhibits a maximum of 1.8% relative error, for a sensing element value variation of 10 Ohm. Sensing linearity is assessed via R2 at up to 0.9995, while sensitivity reaches 57.71 us/Ohm.

verdict.summary: Prototype PCB readout for a small-variation resistive sensor built from off-the-shelf parts, with simple circuit equations validated by measurement; low self-citation, limitations noted, no artifacts.

(7), the on-time as timer difference times timer period, is trivially expressible in words but is ordinary arithmetic, not notation dressing up a data structure, and is not counted as a theater pattern.

27 references; verifiable self-citations: [14] Serbanescu et al., the CAS 2020 conditioning circuit (directly related) and [20] Serban et al., the target humidity sensor (directly related). A modest but honest prototype paper whose claims match its evidence. Formalism is appropriate for a Level 1 system. Weaknesses are the emulated sensing element and no released firmware or design files.

paper.title: Fabrication of Fresnel lenses operating as image correcting optical components for long infrared imaging systems
paper.abstract: We present the technological processes required to fabricate silicon Fresnel lenses with sixteen discrete depth levels operating as corrector optical components for long infrared imaging systems. In order to configure the discrete surface of the lenses, four separated photolithographic processes each one of them followed by deep reactive ion etching were used. In order to detach the configured lenses presenting a disk like shape from the wafer, a DRIE Bosch deep etching process was employed. Finally, an antireflective layer consisting of a nanostructured surface was configured on both sides of the lenses in order to improve the transmission in LWIR spectral range. The geometrical parameters of the fabricated Fresnel lenses were determined by white light interferometry method and it was found that they are in good agreement with the design specifications. The optical and scanning electron microscopy measurements reveal a high quality of the optical surface with a low value of roughness. The spectral characteristics of the lenses in the LWIR spectral region reveal a transmission of above 70%.

paper.title: Investigations of the Fabricated Nothing On Insulator Nanodevices as Metal-Air-Metal variant - NOI-MAM
paper.abstract: This paper presents some investigations of an experimental Nothing On Insulator device, made in the Metal-Air-Metal (NOI-MAM) variant. The vacuum nanodevices are potential candidates for tera-Hertz applications. The investigations concern the fabrication processes, measurements of the output characteristics and simulations of the NOI-MAM devices. Two metallic nanowires are considered instead of two semiconductor nano-islands for Source and Drain. Air molecules in normal conditions inside a gap of maximum 36 nm size represents the "Nothing" area. The electron-beam lithography technology or AFM sectioning by tips are investigated by SEM and AFM analysis. The measured and simulated current-voltage curves are investigated for potential applications.

## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Further investigation of the authors' Nothing On Insulator device in a metal-air-metal variant: EBL-defined Cr/Au nanowire gaps of 19-31 nm, an AFM-scratching attempt, measured I-V curves, and Silvaco Atlas simulations of field, lattice temperature and I-V for three gap sizes.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** Experimental fabrication and commercial-simulator study of a previously reported device; no new model or theory.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 0

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 0
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate; there is no formalism.

### Issues
None identified for formalism.

---

## Citation Analysis

29 references, of which 13 are self-citations: C. Ravariu appears on [4], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13], [15], [16], [17], [18], [19], [21], and A. Srinivasulu on [29]. SCR about 45%, above the 30% threshold. Most Ravariu citations concern NOI devices and are topically related. [29] (ULPD pull-up stages for DCVSL) supports a speculative application paragraph and is only marginally related. Reference [20], a paper on chitosan for biomedical use by unrelated authors, is cited in the range "[18-21]" for NOI simulations and has no evident connection to the topic. The introduction also notes that another group "cited our previous work".

---

## Structural Analysis

New evidence is limited: SEM gap measurements, one AFM scratch that did not fully separate the nanowires, I-V curves already partly reported in [17], and Atlas simulations that differ from the measurements. Key premises are asserted rather than shown: that an air gap under 36 nm is equivalent to vacuum, and that the device has potential DCVSL or terahertz applications. The comparison in Fig. 7 overlays digitised points from other papers on mismatched scales. Limitations are acknowledged inline: incomplete AFM separation, and simulation/experiment discrepancies attributed to heating. No data or simulation decks are released.

---

## Conclusion

An incremental report on a device line dominated by the lead author's own prior work. Formalism is not a concern. The self-citation ratio exceeds the disqualifying threshold, and the application claims outrun the evidence.
